newsitem.title: UK: BT's Vallance calls for calm over MCI.
newsitem.headline: BT's Vallance calls for calm over MCI.

text.p: Sir Iain Vallance, chairman of British Telecommunications Plc, called for calm on Wednesday amid shareholder concern about a profit warning from its proposed merger partner MCI Communications Corp of the U.S.

At a crucial annual meeting in Edinburgh, Vallance dismissed out of hand a call from one shareholder for the resignation of BT chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield for not spotting potential problems with MCI's strategy to break into local U.S. markets.

"The important thing at the moment is that we take time to look sensibly and thoroughly at the U.S. market...(that we) are calm, analyse and act in the best interests of shareholders," Vallance told a packed auditorium of shareholders.

BT was keen to emphasise that a thorough review to be launched into MCI's investment and loss projections will be conducted together with MCI executives and says that until the review is completed, it cannot give explicit guidance as to its implications.

Vallance reiterated that the U.S. market and BT's relationship with MCI continued to be strategically important, and said he fully endorsed MCI's call for free and genuine competition in the $100 billion U.S. local telecoms market.
"If customers are to reap the full benefit of competition there needs to be effective action by regulators to open markets," he said.
MCI has said it was finding it harder, more expensive and more time-consuming to enter U.S. local markets than it had anticipated.

It blames stalling tactics of local telecom operators and a lack of regulatory control, and says local market losses for this year could reach $800 million, more than twice previous forecasts. Losses in 1998 could be even higher.
BT points to the fluid nature of the fast-changing U.S. telecoms market, and says information given to shareholders previously to approve the $20 billion merger was the best available at the time.
"We never said this was going to be easy," chief executive Bonfield told shareholders.
But Vallance praised the courage and skill of MCI, which is America's second-biggest long-distance telecoms carrier, in going after new markets.

Some analysts have questioned why neither BT nor MCI took more heed when AT&T, America's biggest telecoms company, made a similar trading statement about the problems of entering local U.S. markets in March.
But BT says only that MCI had a different view of things at that time.
The BT-MCI merger, dubbed Concert Plc, still awaits final U.S. regulatory clearance from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), which is expected in the autumn.
Some analysts believe MCI's trading statement last Thursday might have more to do with posturing to try and force the FCC to open U.S. local markets more quickly.
